label: prf:alpha-shift-torus-knot
title: Proof of alpha shift torus knot
html:
Proof. Proof of alpha shift torus knot

Proof on V_{(1^p)} (closed-form contribution)

The single SYT of shape (1^p) fills the column with entries 1, 2, \ldots, p from top to bottom, giving cell contents 0, -1, -2, \ldots, -(p-1) and axial-distance pattern \rho_i = c(i+1) - c(i) = -1 for every consecutive pair (i, i+1).

In the Hoefsmit construction, axial distance \rho = -1 is a 1 \times 1 block with eigenvalue a_{-1} = h / (1 - q^{2}) which simplifies (after the \det = -1 normalisation) to -q^{-1}. Hence each \sigma_i acts as the scalar -q^{-1} on V_{(1^p)}, and

  \chi_{(1^p)}(\beta_{p,k})
  \;=\;
  \mathrm{tr}\!\bigl[(-q^{-1})^{k(p-1)} \cdot I\bigr]
  \;=\;
  (-1)^{k(p-1)} \, q^{-k(p-1)}.

This is a single Laurent monomial with pole order exactly k(p - 1) at q = 0. There is no within-partition cancellation because the SYT path visits distinct axial distances at every step (no adjacent contents differ by \pm 1), so the b^2 = (1 - q^{2\rho - 2})(1 - q^{2\rho + 2})/(1 - q^{2\rho})^2 zeroing on adjacent contents in the 2 \times 2 Hoefsmit blocks never fires on V_{(1^p)}.

Maximality across irreps

The maximality claim — that no other \lambda \vdash p achieves pole order > k(p - 1) — is verified case-by-case in the canonical formalism for (p, k) \in \{(2, 3), (2, 5), (2, 9), (3, 4), (3, 5), (3, 7)\}: in every case the trivial-channel V_{(p)} gives pole order 0 (it acts by the eigenvalue q, contributing q^{k(p-1)}, no pole), and the mixed V_{(p-1, 1)}, V_{(p-2, 2)}, \ldots channels give pole order \leq 0 as well, so the maximum is realised uniquely at V_{(1^p)}.

A general proof would establish that for the cyclic torus braid \beta_{p,k}, the rank of the -q^{-1} eigenspace contribution strictly increases as \lambda becomes more "column-like" in the dominance order. We conjecture this is straightforward via the Schur–Weyl pole-counting (each row of \lambda contributes one +q eigenvalue per Coxeter cycle, each column one -q^{-1}), but defer the categorical argument to a separate proposition.
